body: I'd argue this increases the mental load for using this template and requires contributors to keep track of what they need in different cases, I'm not convinced this is an improvement

> I'd argue this increases the mental load for using this template and requires contributors to keep track of what they need in different cases, I'm not convinced this is an improvement

They already have to 'keep track of it' because they'll have to set the boolean on `LocalVector`'s side. 
Personally, I think that makes for higher mental load model, because when I call `resize` on a `LocalVector`, I have to check the `LocalVector` template arguments to see if it's a "slow" resize with default values set, or a "fast" resize where they're ignored.
Most users will just call `resize(3)` without template arguments, but where it matters, it's better to be explicit. And, like I mentioned, there will be cases where you'll want a defaulted resize in one method, and a fast resize in the next.

This also breaks compatibility with godot-cpp, which is somewhat relevant, as this class exists there and should be kept in sync, and changes with that would break compatibility for those uses

For the mental load it involves reviewers and contributors making sure this is respected when it is used, which currently doesn't require that, but instead just requires that someone has that set on the declaration and then any use is guaranteed, which is where contributors use it

> This also breaks compatibility with godot-cpp, which is somewhat relevant, as this class exists there and should be kept in sync, and changes with that would break compatibility for those uses

That's true, I'm not sure I have a great solution for that. But I don't think many people will be using the parameter right now, when even in all of Godot it is only used 4 times (or ~ 8 times if you count tight vectors). We'd probably have to make a note of that in godot-cpp 4.5 changelogs. But I'll tag the GDExtension team (/ @dsnopek) for review :)

Edit: New idea, it could be ignored and marked deprecated, both here and in godot-cpp. That would help avoid update problems.

> For the mental load it involves reviewers and contributors making sure this is respected when it is used, which currently doesn't require that, but instead just requires that someone has that set on the declaration and then any use is guaranteed, which is where contributors use it

It is currently used in only 4 places, so I'm not sure that matters. Besides, correct is more important than fast. The current model risks `resize` being called on a `force_trivial` vector, with the reviewer possibly expecting a defaulted resize, because the `force_trivial` parameter is not explicitly set on the `resize` call. This would be a bug, and is more important to avoid than potential speed issues (that may not even matter until measured) :)

> And, like I mentioned, there will be cases where you'll want a defaulted resize in one method, and a fast resize in the next.

Is there an example of this in practice? :thinking: 

Have to admit I'm also tending towards keeping the current system, I can't think of where I've ever needed to hot swap between `force_trivial` on different resizes so far, but perhaps there is something we have not thought of.

> > And, like I mentioned, there will be cases where you'll want a defaulted resize in one method, and a fast resize in the next.
> 
> Is there an example of this in practice? 🤔
> 
> Have to admit I'm also tending towards keeping the current system, I can't think of where I've ever needed to hot swap between `force_trivial` on different resizes so far, but perhaps there is something we have not thought of.

Of course! I have to admit, it took me a bit to find an example I was fully happy with, because `LocalVector` and `resize` are both not used all too often, in conjunction with types that are trivially destructible and not trivially constructible just doesn't happen all too much right now 😅
But I did find an example that kinda fulfills the needed criteria - I think it will do for demonstration purposes. There exists `Point` for navigation:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/2303ce843a362cf5497ca3336451de23793eb711/modules/navigation/nav_utils_3d.h#L75-L78

`Point` has default values (through both fields), and is thus not trivially constructible, but it is trivially destructible.
`Polygon` has a `LocalVector` of those:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/2303ce843a362cf5497ca3336451de23793eb711/modules/navigation/nav_utils_3d.h#L107-L108

In `nav_region_3d.cpp`, `points` are resized and then assigned. Sometimes, not all elements are assigned:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/2303ce843a362cf5497ca3336451de23793eb711/modules/navigation/nav_region_3d.cpp#L248
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/2303ce843a362cf5497ca3336451de23793eb711/modules/navigation/nav_region_3d.cpp#L265-L274

It is also called from `nav_map_builder_3d.cpp`, and immediately assigned:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/2303ce843a362cf5497ca3336451de23793eb711/modules/navigation/3d/nav_map_builder_3d.cpp#L347-L353

Both locations could benefit from a non-defaulted `resize` (at least the latter would, and the former might depending on why sometimes elements aren't explicitly assigned).

However, neither `.cpp` file really owns `points`. It would be odd to make this optimization at the field declaration, because the `resize` calling code knows why the defaults aren't needed here, but the declaration has no idea how it might be initialized and filled later. 
I hope this illustrates why this change just makes sense from a coupling perspective.


There are also tons of examples of resize being called with trivially destructible but not trivially constructible types, like `AABB`:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/2303ce843a362cf5497ca3336451de23793eb711/scene/resources/animation.cpp#L50-L53

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/2303ce843a362cf5497ca3336451de23793eb711/scene/resources/animation.h#L355

Here, `compression.bounds` is resized, which initializes all its entries to all-zero (`AABB` / `Vector3` default).
Then, immediately, the entries are replaced, making the `resize` call unnecessarily slow.
It would be possible to re-declare `compression.bounds` as `LocalVector<AABB, uint32_t, true>`, but that would be unnecessarily intrusive (as discussed above).

I've got another that for me highlights how `force_trivial` could be useful for `Vector`:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/2303ce843a362cf5497ca3336451de23793eb711/core/math/a_star.cpp#L462-L476

Here, the vector is resized, and the entries are initialized to all-zero (`Vector3` default). Immediately, all entries are replaced with values in a loop. If `force_zero` were available on `resize`, it would be possible to slightly speed up the function here. However, it would be impossible to declare `force_trivial` on `Vector`, because that would make it incompatible with `PackedVector3Array`. If we were to add it, it would _have_ to be added to `resize`.

Ah, yes, it reminds me I actually brought up the resize inefficiency with constructors a few weeks ago (can't remember if RC or on a PR).

This is a common pattern, resize then fill all the elements.

Also wondering about an alternative:

* Keep the `force_trivial` on the `LocalVector`
* Allow overriding the setting on resize (i.e. if you set `force_trivial` param on the resize it overrides the `LocalVector` default, if not it uses the default)
* Alternatively have a different function name like `resize_trivial()` or some such for code clarity (that acts as a wrapper)

That would seem to cover both cases while still retaining the convenience for people who don't want to call it on each resize? :thinking:

This is an interesting solution!
I'd argue it would still keep the mental overhead higher than needed, because you always have to remember whether you're dealing with a defaulting or non-defaulting `LocalVector` right now.
But I'd be OK with it, it _would_ solve my main issue with it.
Edit: And it would keep complete backward compatibility, which is nice too.

I think my major concern with losing the `force_trivial` for `LocalVector` is that it _currently_ makes the intention clear for the container. You want to use it in a C like fashion, and you don't want any "c++ BS" (pardon my french).

There is a real danger in terms of maintenance, if this is put onto `only` the resize function, that someone will make a later function or changes that don't respect the `force_trivial` intention, or things could get "lost in translation".

Out of the versions so far I would (personally) favour the addition of a `resize_trivial()` function (or maybe using a defaulted enum if preferred, `bools` are kind of hard to read in often used functions imo).

Be nice to hear some more feedback e.g. @AThousandShips , probably one for some bikeshedding maybe even in a core meeting.

My concern here is mainly:
* Establishing the need for this change in the first place, i.e. the demand for doing the specific patterns of different resize
* The impact of separating the behavior in other cases mentioned like `push_back`
* The impact on extensions, as we have to have parity, where breaking compatibility matters, unlike core
* The possible impact, both in mental overhead for reviewers and contributors in ensuring this is used correctly, and the risk of missing cases where it needs to be used and that causing performance issues due to it being difficult to track what specific container is used or not

Mainly I think it's a bit of a big and disruptive change that needs to be assessed and bikeshedded to ensure it is worth the cost, and I'm personally not convinced that the benefits outweigh the costs

I agree with lawnjelly here that I think it'd be better to keep the current system and add options to change the beahvior where needed, this would be the least disruptive and risky, and I'd suggest having both changes, i.e. `resize_trivial/nontrivial` that ignore the template argument
Despite where to place `force_trival`, I think simplifying `push_back` and `remove_at` code should be welcome and easy to merge (if it doesn't hurt performance). Might worth a seperate PR.

Personally, I would leave force_trivial as-is and just add a new method to resize without calling constructors. Then we can get the benefit of explicitness where it would be beneficial without breaking compatibility or adding more complexity for ordinary users of the container

Alright, I'm seeing somewhat of a consensus over keeping the template parameter on `LocalVector`. I'd still prefer to remove it, but fair arguments have been made, and my main motivation is elsewhere anyway.

I've uploaded a new version which keeps `ensure_zero` on `LocalVector`. In turn, `LocalVector::resize` now offers both `ensure_zero` and `force_trivial` behavior, supplied through a new enum that conveys intent better (imo).
I'll update the PR description accordingly.
Let me know what you think!

I would personally probably benefit from a slightly simpler language way of doing this too (like `resize()` and `resize_trivial()`). :blush:

I agree the enum names are a bit more esoteric, but they are also more accurate than the named functions we've had so far 😅
Here's what I may name them if we didn't have an enum:

```c++
resize<OnAllocInit::DEFAULT>(x)
resize(x) // just the default resize behavior

resize<OnAllocInit::ALWAYS>(x)
resize_zeroed(x) // the name we have
resize_and_init(x) // the name we probably should have, although it almost implies resize() doesn't init values...

resize<OnAllocInit::AVOID>(x)
resize_trivial(x) // what you're proposing
resize_avoid_initializing_if_possible(x) // the name we probably should have
```

The reason `zeroed` is technically inaccurate is that it's technically only zeroing structs that are all-zero. Calling `resize_zeroed()` on a `Vector<Color>` will not actually zero it, it will keep `alpha` at 1, as set by the default. This is misunderstandable.
We have the same problem with `resize_uninitialized`: It will only actually not initialize entries if this is allowed by the type. Not initializing a type that is not trivially destructible would be unsafe for the container. So we ignore the request to not initialize it if it would be unsafe for the item type.

Woh, you are right, that current resize zeroed is strange and doesn't seem to make a lot of sense. :face_with_diagonal_mouth: 

I'm not sure I get what resize zeroed is used for exactly in Godot 4.

I wonder if the answer could be using more `static_asserts`?

Call `resize_zeroed()` on something that cannot be zero constructed should maybe static assert, and it should be `resize()`?

Calling `resize_trivial()` on something that cannot be trivially destructed should also static assert maybe?

Having `resize_zeroed` be "sometimes zero and sometimes don't" seems like craziness.

> I'm not sure I get what resize zeroed is used for exactly in Godot 4.

As far as I've heard, `resize_zeroed` was introduced to replace `.resize()` calls from GDScript because resizing e.g. a `PackedFloatArray` and then seeing garbage data in new elements of was seen as a bug. For all the types it was used for, the name made sense.

> I wonder if the answer could be using more static_asserts?

This would also be possible. We could e.g. have a `OnAllocInit::Never` which statically asserts that the type is trivially destructible. That would probably eclipse most uses of `OnAllocInit::Avoid` by user code, but it wouldn't be usable from the "resize-then-fill" pattern from templated code, which would only be able to make use of `OnAllocInit::AVOID`. 

> Having resize_zeroed be "sometimes zero and sometimes don't" seems like craziness.

Fully agreed, that's why I'd like to rename it 😄
The actual functionality of it makes sense to me: We're splitting functionality into 3 camps, either:
- always initialize to a known value, or
-  avoid initializing if possible for performance reasons, or
-  just do whatever C++ would do when declaring this variable without initializing it explicitly. 

All 3 are sometimes useful so I think it does make sense to keep the behavior itself as is. I'd just like to rename it to more accurately reflect what it does.

So maybe it's just agreeing between all of us on names that are easily understandable. Here's a stab at some names: :thinking: 
* safe / safe_init (c++ initialize or zero if no constructor) e.g. `safe_resize`
* regular (no name), just use regular c++ init e.g. `resize`
* trivial, do nothing, static assert if used on the wrong type (non trivially destructable) e.g. `trivial_resize`

(or enums, but some good names seems to be key.)

Now it's explained, I don't think your suggestions are bad but I maybe they would benefit from qualifying:
```
	DEFAULT_INIT
	ALWAYS_INIT
	AVOID_INIT
```

Well, perhaps me being accustomed to `OnAllocInit` as an enum name comes from my Obj-C background, where we used to do `[[MyClass alloc] init]` all the time :D Perhaps we could find a better name for the enum though?

I do think naming the symbols based on the behavior, i.e. "always init new values", "avoid init of new values if possible" and "init or not based on c++ default behavior", is a good way to describe what is happening (and perhaps "never init and fail if this is unsafe"). I want to avoid inventing new words for this if possible, and I'm having trouble with the ones you chose in particular as well (with "safe" because all cases are safe, and with "trivial" because what "trivial" means changes depending on the context).

Yeah it sounds like a good subject for bikeshedding, maybe we can vote in the core meeting or something like that.
As long as the words are clear it's all good in my book. :+1: 
(the _trivial_ BTW just came from pre-existing Godot use for containers, I'm not sure on the origins)

I've made adjustments as discussed in the core meeting:
- `OnAllocInit::AVOID` is replaced with `OnAllocInit::NEVER`: When used with a type that wouldn't be safe to 'trivially' initialize, it will statically complain instead of defaulting to initializing it.
- The templated `resize` using the enum is not exposed. Instead, 3 functions are offered:
    - `resize`, using either `OnAllocInit::DEFAULT` or `OnAllocInit::NEVER`, depending on if `force_trivial` is set.
    - `resize_zeroed`, analogous to `Vector.resize_zeroed`, initializing all elements. This is only available for types where this makes sense (zero constructible).
    - `resize_trivial`: analogous to using a `force_trivial` vector, resize but don't initialize the elements. It will complain if this would be unsafe for the type.

I have added some extra checks, and I do think it's now a bit easier to understand than before :)

Edit: I had to adjust the `PackedColorArray` `.resize` binding to use `.resize` instead of `resize_zeroed`, because `Color` is not zero constructible (it uses alpha=1 as the default value). The new behavior is more consistent with how `Color` usually constructs, but it is a behavior change.
If I didn't want to change behavior here, I'd either need to remove the `is_trivially_constructible` assertion (which would be semantically questionable), or add a separate `is_zero_default_constructible` type. This might be useful anyway, but it's kind of out of scope, so I chose to just 'fix' the `PackedColorArray` resize operator. Let me know what you think.

Sorry forgot this PR as I was away weekend. This is getting much better.

I must admit I'm still not sold on `resize_zeroed()` versus `resize_safe()`, and whether we _actually need_ a `resize_zeroed` function.

From the description, it sounds like `zeroed` was introduced because users wanted arrays to always be either constructed to default, or zeroed (if a simple type). The way I'm reading this, the problem seems more likely to be that this functionality was improperly named. As is the case of your `Color` example.

If this is the case, then simply renaming to `resize_safe` (or similar) might be a better solution.

_The reason I suggested the `safe` terminology earlier is because it conveys the user intent (even though other versions may still be considered "safe" in other ways). "Safe" languages for beginners do this kind of thing, they always initialize arrays rather than risk uninitialized data, at the cost of performance._

The use cases of `resize_zeroed` itself seem more limited. How many times is it actually used / required (versus `resize_safe`) in the codebase? :thinking: 

If it is an optimization for e.g. `Vector3` to allow memsetting instead of calling the constructor by element, we could have a compile time checkable thing similar to `is_zero_constructible` that allows the resizer to just memset instead of calling constructors. In which case we might not even need the `resize_zeroed` function.

Worst case, we should remember we _could_ just `resize_trivial()` and then memset manually if it was that important for a rare case.

Just some thoughts, maybe there are some cases for `zeroed` which I'm not aware of.

Hrm, I think i get it, but wouldn't the user intent actually be "resize with known values" instead of "resize in a safe manner"? As mentioned before, _all_ resize operations should be (and are) completely safe. It just affects if the default value is garbage or known.

> The use cases of `resize_zeroed` itself seem more limited. How many times is it actually used / required (versus `resize_safe`) in the codebase? 🤔
>

In which case we might not even need the `resize_zeroed` function.

This is not about optimization.
The optimization of using `memset` _is_ already being applied (where possible). It's about whether trivial types that normally aren't initialized by C++ should be initialized.

> Worst case, we should remember we _could_ just `resize_trivial()` and then memset manually if it was that important for a rare case.

That's definitely true.
 
I ran some experiments today and have a few new insights. Putting it together with your thoughts, how would you feel about this:

- Add `resize_safe` / `resize_and_init` / `some_other_name` which initializes all elements to known (default) values.
- Add `resize_trivial` which doesn't initialize any elements. It statically fails if the element type is not trivially destructible (i.e. unsafe).
- Deprecate `resize` (and remove it in a follow-up PR).
- Remove `resize_zeroed` and replace uses with `resize_safe`

With this setup, `resize_safe` _always_ initializes elements to known values. And `resize_trivial` _never_ initializes elements to known values. In this way, we may eliminate a whole class of bugs (where people forget to initialize elements), because they'll consciously have to decide to use `resize_trivial` in cases where they'll initialize elements manually later).

The corresponding `enum` values would be `OnAllocInit::ALWAYS` and `OnAllocInit::NEVER` (with `DEFAULT` gone).

I guess moving on from your logic above of maybe only actually needing two versions, it might make sense to just make the default `resize` the safe version without the suffix:

* `resize` (safe version)
* `resize_trivial`

And then allow overriding the `resize` version if `force_trivial` is set for the template.

This would mean however probably going through hand and finding any existing resize cases for trivial types and possibly replacing them with `resize_trivial` manually. They all should I suppose work _by definition_ with `resize_trivial` as that is what is technically happening already with these vectors.

You might be able to use a static assert or `[[deprecated]]` trick to spit out all the line numbers of existing resizes using trivial types. :thinking: 

This is basically exactly as you suggest above but just replacing the existing `resize` with `resize_safe` version.

> I guess moving on from your logic above of maybe only actually needing two versions, it might make sense to just make the default resize the safe version without the suffix:

This would work. But I'd feel more comfortable if the initializing resize function name (`resize_safe`) would make it clear that it is initializing all elements, because it would make it easier to identify cases where `resize_trivial` would be more appropriate.
I'm only realizing now that this would make `force_trivial` obsolete, but that makes sense to me: When you're making a resize, you _need_ to know whether or not you're initializing elements - because if you don't, you probably have to initialize them "by hand" immediately. It would be possible to softly phase `force_trivial` out, without removing it, by making setting it to true complain.

> You might be able to use a static assert or [[deprecated]] trick to spit out all the line numbers of existing resizes using trivial types. 🤔

Makes sense. If any were expecting a trivial resize before, switching behavior with the same function name would be a regression. Another reason why I'd prefer the `resize_safe` and `resize_trivial` pair over `resize` and `resize_trivial`; there's no doubt which one it's going to do :)

> Another reason why I'd prefer the resize_safe and resize_trivial pair over resize and resize_trivial; there's no doubt which one it's going to do :)

I'm personally not massively against this, maybe we can put it to a vote (maybe in core meeting).

Ok, I tried to implement the proposed interfaces today (`resize` for "always initialize elements", `resize_uninitialized` for "never initialize elements), and get rid of the current "resize" functionality). But I found that across the 2500 calls to `resize`, it's impossible to change the functionality without regressions.
I thought it would be possible / safe to introduce `resize_legacy` and change all calls there, to slowly build them down until we can finally get rid of them fully, but i tried this and my attempt failed. I'm not sure what was going wrong, but in all likeliness it was just too complex of a PR to work.

I will put this one on hold until some surrounding code progresses to make this task easier (in case you're wondering, take a look at all my open PRs 😅).

I've updated the PR to reflect the latest wisdom from recent core meetings:
- `resize_initialized` will _always_ initialized elements
- `resize_uninitialized` will _never_ initialize elements
- `resize` keeps the same, wonky behavior that it has now

This PR serves as an entry point to changing existing callers to use either `resize_initialize` or `resize_uninitialized` explicitly.
When all of them are decided, we can delete `resize` altogether, and rename `resize_initialized` to `resize`. However, that's for a follow-up, as this PR is complex enough as it is.

I hope this addresses all the concerns we've had before about this change :)
